Page 6 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program While the above design is preliminary, it captures some of the primary design concepts outlined by KEK, SLAC and others. The structure is joined using two welding processes: direct copper electron beam welding (EBW) and stainless steel tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding. Auxiliary components such as waveguide flange are vacuum brazed as copper/stainless sub-assemblies. A bill of materials of all the sub-components is listed below with almost all the machining risk constrained to the 4x RF quad parts. Part Quantity Comments RF quad 4 Linear EB welding WG-stem 4 2 part brazed stainless/copper assembly EB welded WG-flange 4 X3 part brazed stainless/copper assembly TIG welded Vacuum-stem 10 2 part brazed stainless/copper assembly EB welded CF flange 10 Off-shelf part TIG welded Total parts 54 The manufacturing strategy is based on a a series of copper EB welds which are listed in Figure 6-top right. Namely EB weld #1 is four, length-wise linear welds which join the quadrants together while two EB weld #2 close out front and back of the quadrant structure. Next EB weld #3 is composed of four plug-type welds joining the brazed copper/stainless steel waveguide stem to the upper section of the structure. Finally, ten plug- type EB weld #4 are joing brazed copper/stainless steel vacuum stems around the perimeter of the structure, with serve either as beam or vacuum ports. In the following process, a series of manual stainless-steel to stainless TIG welds are performed, joining the waveguide flange to the waveguide stem (TIG#1) or the vacuum flange to the vacuum stem (TIG#2). This two-step EB then TIG welding approach addresses a significant geometric challenge of the structure, which is that it is difficult for the electron beam to weld beneath the shadow of a flange. This approach addresses this issue by EB welding brazed copper/stainless steel stems to various ports on the structure. The flanges can then be TIG welded using stainless steel to stainless steel welding. The EB welding process will take a full 8 hrs, with a pumpdown beginning the day before. Special consideration regarding handling, assembly and EB welding setup will be needed to account for the weight of the structure (250kg) and to consolidate the number of setups within the EBW machine. With the device fixtured onto an axially rotating remotely controllable fixture, it may be possible to reduce the number of setups to 3 total, one for all 4x longitudinal welds, 4x coupler welds and 8x side stems and a setup each for the end joints and stems.
